thread.title: Ron Johnson discusses retail in a Q&A - Barron's

title: Ron Johnson discusses retail in a Q&A - Barron's
text:
A Q&A With Retail Executive Ron Johnson By Jan. 4, 2019 7:10 p.m. ET Order Reprints Ron Johnson Photograph by Peter Prato Text size
From reimagining Target as “Tarjay,” to inventing the Apple store, Ron Johnson has been at the center of some of the most exciting retail trends of the past 35 years. The 60-year-old now runs a Silicon Valley start-up called Enjoy that he thinks can change retail . He recently spoke with Barron’s about how retail has changed, where he sees the next big opportunity, and why his short stint as CEO of J.C. Penney was such a bust.
Barron’s: When did you get started in retail, and what was the industry like then?
Ron Johnson: When I came out of Harvard Business School in 1984, I decided to devote my career to retail. If you go back to 1984, it wasn’t that strange a choice. At that time, the big boxes were just being built, like Best Buy (BBY) stores and Toys “R” Us. There was a lot of innovation in retail and a lot of venture capital going into retail. And so it was a good time to get it on the ground floor of an industry that I thought would appeal to me for a lifetime.
My first job was with a Minneapolis company, which is now Target (TGT). I spent 15 years there. That was Chapter One of my career.
What were people’s shopping habits like at the time?
At that time, everyone cared about value, but there was all this segmentation. People thought about Walmart (WMT) the way people have thought about Amazon (AMZN) for the last decade. How can you compete with it? They’ve got the lowest prices, they’ve got all this technology that drives their operation.
When I joined Target, there were 11 regional discount stores where ultimately today there are two, Target and Walmart. At Target, we concluded rather than trying to compete head on, we would try to be different.
At Target, we did that through merchandising and marketing. We created an identity that became known as Tarjay. It became a hip place to shop.
Did you come up with Tarjay?
Customers did. I don’t know if anyone knows where it came from, but it became an expression, like a nickname. It captured what Target was. It was like people from France, you know, they’re just hipper, they’re more sophisticated, they’re more interesting.
Someone who’s on a budget didn’t have to be embarrassed about where they shop. They could say, “Look what I found. I want to tell everybody that I’ve shopped there.” We carved out a very unique position in a crowded retail marketplace. We really made an effort to do all unique merchandise that was elevated to get things that you might find at a department store or at Williams-Sonoma or Crate & Barrel. You could find something that was just as good at Target for a great value.
And you were at Target when you got the call from Apple, the king of all consumer products. It was 2000 when you joined.
At the time Apple (AAPL) had a very small market share, it was 3% of the computer industry. Best Buy wouldn’t even carry Apple products. They were sold through mom-and-pop retailers. At that time, people would buy PCs through Gateway or CompUSA. When we launched the stores, Gateway was shutting down [Gateway closed its last stores in 2004]. Nobody thought Apple should open stores. Why would you pay high-price rent for something people only buy every three or four years? Gateway couldn’t make money selling 97% of the computers. Why would Apple open stores with that small of a market share?
So why do it?
Steve [Jobs] concluded that Apple had to open its own stores to have a chance to win or compete. Because to really understand the value of Apple’s products, you’ve got to get under the hood, below the surface. You have to really explain to people how the operating system works, how the software works.
If we’re going to enrich someone’s life, we’ve got to locate the stores in high-traffic areas where they live their lives. We’ve got to provide ongoing support and help. We created stores with things like Genius Bars and one-on-one training and theaters. When you bought a Mac, we stood behind it. Not through a warranty, but through the ability to learn how to use it. Steve knew and I intuitively believed if Apple is going to win, it had to be something completely unique and new and fresh that solved the problem, which was how you appreciate the extraordinary potential for a Mac to improve your life.
So then you went from a rising retailer to a more troubled one. How did you get the call at J.C. Penney?
They were looking for a new board member. I went to the board interviews in 2011, and the board concluded, “Well, I wonder if Ron would want to be CEO of the company.” So I joined J.C. Penney (JCP) in 2012.
And leave such a good job at Apple?
The challenge to reimagine a department store was very exciting to me. I always considered myself a retail guy even though I worked at Apple. I had had this wonderful experience being on the Target team when we reimagined the discount store. I was at Apple when we invented the great retail store. I thought, well, I’ve never had to turn around something. What if we could reimagine a hundred-year old department store and make it relevant again? Running Apple had become a hobby. I had done it for 12 years and we had stores in 13 countries, they were all flourishing. How do you try to do something that no one else would even attempt to do?
What did the stores look like when you got there and what did you want to do?
I wanted to get J.C. Penney to become a desirable store for a younger family. The Penney customer had matured. They were older. Young people didn’t shop at J.C. Penney. So how do you appeal to the next generation customer? You’ve got to reinvent how they experienced the store.
Families probably don’t want to sit there and look through circulars and clip coupons all day. A young person wants the best price every day. So we went to everyday pricing. We brought in new brands. A young person doesn’t want to go to a huge store that’s disorganized. They want to have someone help edit the assortment for them. We did all of these new presentations, created the store-within-a-store like the Levi’s shop. We were going to reimagine the store.
I told them that when we stop using promotional pricing, our sales are going to drop at least 15 percent for a year. We’ve got to do that, but then we’ll grow, because we’ll be differentiated. We ended up pulling back from all this bad promotional behavior. Well, the month we did that, sales went down, and I discovered that the board, the investors, the employees did not have the stomach for change. That’s really hard.
I was a really terrible fit for J.C. Penney. I was told the company wanted change. They had no interest in change. So I resigned in 2013. [JC Penney and board members did not respond to requests for comment]
It was an interesting way to try to solve the big problem: How can any of these stores make it when the internet is taking over shopping?
The internet isn’t taking over shopping, the internet is becoming a part of shopping. If you look today, this is the first time in 20 years the physical retailers have the upper hand, and they will for the next decade. Amazon is the one in the tough competitive position right now.
Why is that?
Amazon’s strength is that it has a broad assortment of moderate-priced merchandise that people go to for the convenience of shopping. And they’ve got these great programs like Prime and free shipping over a certain threshold, so it’s a very convenient place to shop. Well, that’s what Target and Walmart have always been—a broad assortment and a convenient place to shop. But for years Target and Walmart didn’t take the internet as seriously as they should, but now they have.
How so?
If you look at it today, Target and Walmart have stores within seven miles of your home. Target and Walmart have 50 warehouses right in the middle of where people live their lives. You can order online and they’ll deliver from that store. They can deliver foods cheaper and faster to customers. You can buy online and pickup in store or buy online and return to the store. It’s a much better holistic experience than Amazon. Target and Walmart’s online sales are going to be doubling four or five times over the nine years. They’ve got a competitive advantage and for the first time in 20 years that’s become obvious to everyone.
I live in the Valley, which is the center of online shopping in the U.S. The hardest place to park is Stanford Shopping Center. Go figure that out.
Physical stores have had to reimagine the in-store environment and how does it work with the online experience, but they’re all learning to do that. Now, the balance is shifting again where it’s kind of fun to go to the store because I discover things.
So now you’ve got a new company that has a different take on retail, right? Tell me about Enjoy.
What we’re doing at Enjoy is we’re inventing the mobile retail store. The way to think about it is there’s two frontiers in retail that have existed. There’s the physical store, which has a thousand-year head start. The same landlord has leased the space the Apple store occupies in London on Regent Street for a thousand years. We’re about 24 years into the next frontier, which is online shopping. Online shopping is about a device to a doorstep. You order on a device and it’s delivered to your doorstep.
What we do is we bring the store through the door, with a person who will create an experience like you received in the store in the comfort of your own home. Someone makes sure it’s the right item. They set it up, get it up and running for you. All for free.
Before this you had two choices. You could go to Best Buy, to the old physical store, take it home and figure out how to unbox it and go read the instruction manual. Or you could order it online from Amazon. It will show up in a couple of days at your doorstep and hopefully no one steals it, and then you have to set it up yourself.
With Enjoy you can have it delivered to you by a really kind person and set up for the same price, in three hours or less. That’s a pretty magical experience, right?
If it’s free to the consumer, that means the company has to pay. Why would they do that? What’s in it for AT&T, for instance?
AT&T (T) wants to move from being a phone company to being an entertainment company. They want to make sure you know how you can watch television on your phone through Direct TV now. They don’t want to just ship a device, they want to talk to you about what you can do on the device. We partner with companies like Google (GOOGL), AT&T, Sonos (SONO).
We generate extraordinary value beyond shipping. When we bring a product and get it up and running, they don’t return it. If you ordered a black phone and got a gray one, it’s no problem. Because we bring the black one, too. Nobody’s calling the call center. We function as the call center. You’ve got a person inserted into the equation who’s trained. When you go to the store to buy a phone, you probably buy a case and a screen saver too. We’re a mobile store, we bring all the accessories with us too. When you put it all together we become a very high-touch profit-generating channel.
Because online shopping is too impersonal?
It’s all about giving people a connection, like what the Apple stores did. Apple created a connection to the brand through a physical place and a person. We provide that human connection in the comfort of your home for our partners. There will be a lot of times when we don’t want that, and that’s what Amazon, Target, and Walmart will be best at. With some products I just want convenience. But when my purchase really counts, like a smart-home product, I’m going to value an experience. I want to learn how to do things I didn’t know how to do. When you order online, you’re on your own.
If you look at the physical world, there are convenience stores and there are experience stores. The Apple store is an experience store. Walmart is a convenience store. In the online world, there should be convenience stores—that’s Amazon—and experience stores. That’s what Enjoy is. We’re now a mobile store that provides an experience.
To me, that’s as interesting as it was when I had to go figure out how do you build an Apple store? How do I use my imagination to reimagine the department store? Now I’m using my imagination with our team to invent the next channel for retail, which I believe is the mobile store.
Thanks, Ron.
